# Google's Four AI Departures: "We Wanted to Build Something Differently"

When four senior researchers leave one of the most well-resourced AI labs in the world to start something new, the interesting question isn't why they left. It's what they think they can build that Google can't.

The departures from DeepMind point to a growing tension in how AI research gets productized — and whether the incentive structures at large companies are compatible with the kind of foundational work that made those companies dominant in the first place.

## What's Actually Happening

At the start of 2025, a group of DeepMind researchers began quietly exploring what it would look like to leave Google and build something independently. By mid-year, four of them had done exactly that.

According to reporting from The New Stack, the researchers involved were working on what DeepMind internally called the "discovery loop" — a research methodology focused on generating novel scientific insights rather than optimizing existing systems. The approach apparently emphasized exploration over exploitation, prioritizing unexpected findings over incremental improvements to production models.

The departures weren't acrimonious. No public disputes, no blog posts about toxic culture. Just a straightforward acknowledgment that they wanted to build something differently.

That phrasing matters. "Differently" suggests the issue wasn't resources or talent — DeepMind has both in abundance. It suggests the issue was *how* the work gets done, what gets prioritized, and what success looks like.

The researchers reportedly believed that the discovery loop methodology was being constrained by Google's product timelines and commercial pressures. Research that didn't map cleanly to near-term product improvements was harder to justify. Work that might take years to pay off — or might not pay off at all — competed for resources against projects with clearer ROI.

This is a familiar dynamic in corporate R&D. The lab that produced the breakthrough gets absorbed into the machine that needs to ship features.

## The Pattern Behind the Departures

Google's AI departures have become a recurring story. The details vary, but the shape is consistent.

In recent years, the company has seen high-profile exits across its AI organizations — not just DeepMind, but Google Brain (before the merger), the Responsible AI team, and various product-focused AI groups. Some left over ethical disagreements. Some left for startups or competitors. Some left to start their own companies.

The discovery loop departures fit a specific variant of this pattern: researchers who aren't frustrated with the company's values or treatment, but with its *velocity* and *focus*. They want to work on harder problems with longer time horizons and less certainty about outcomes.

This is harder to argue with from a corporate governance perspective. Google isn't doing anything wrong by prioritizing products. That's what companies do. But it creates a structural tension with the kind of open-ended research that produced many of Google's advantages in the first place.

[UNVERIFIED] Some industry observers have suggested that Google's internal incentive structures — particularly performance review criteria and promotion committees — increasingly reward shipping features over publishing research. This would align with the discovery loop researchers' stated concerns, but I haven't seen this documented beyond speculation.

## Why Practitioners Should Care

If you're building software in a team that uses AI tooling, you might wonder why internal Google politics matters to you.

Here's why: the incentive structures that push researchers out of big labs shape what tools and models actually get built.

When research teams optimize for product integration, you get incremental improvements to existing capabilities. Faster inference. Better context windows. More efficient fine-tuning. These are genuinely useful, and they matter for day-to-day development work.

When research teams optimize for discovery, you get architectural innovations that change what's possible. Transformers. Reinforcement learning from human feedback. Chain-of-thought prompting. These create entirely new categories of tooling.

The tension between these two modes is real, and the departures from DeepMind suggest that Google may be shifting toward the former. That's not inherently bad — someone needs to make the tools actually work — but it does change what you should expect from Google's AI offerings in the next few years.

If you're evaluating Gemini or other Google AI products for your development workflow, the question is whether you're betting on incremental improvements to current architectures or on breakthrough capabilities. The discovery loop departures suggest that some of the people best positioned to deliver the latter think they can do it better elsewhere.

## What This Means for the Broader Ecosystem

The researchers who left are reportedly starting a new company focused on the discovery loop methodology. Details are sparse, but the implication is that they believe this approach to AI research requires organizational independence — not just a skunkworks project within Google, but a separate entity with different incentives.

This is notable because DeepMind already operates with significant autonomy within Google. If even DeepMind's structure isn't sufficient for the kind of research these people want to do, it raises questions about whether any large company can sustain truly open-ended AI research.

The counterargument is that startups face their own constraints. Funding pressure. Customer demands. The need to ship something before the money runs out. These pressures can be just as distorting as corporate product timelines, and often more existential.

But startups also have advantages for this kind of work. Smaller teams can move faster. There's less coordination overhead. And founders can optimize for whatever they want — including long-term research — as long as they can convince investors to go along.

The interesting question is whether the discovery loop researchers can actually build something that matters outside the Google ecosystem. DeepMind's resources — compute, data, talent density — are hard to replicate. The methodology might be brilliant, but methodologies don't train models.

## The Broader Trend: Labs as Feeder Systems

One way to read these departures is as evidence that big AI labs are becoming feeder systems for startups.

Google, OpenAI, Meta, Anthropic — these organizations train researchers, give them access to cutting-edge problems and infrastructure, and then lose them to ventures that promise more autonomy or upside. It's similar to what happened with early Google employees who left to start their own companies in the 2000s and 2010s.

This isn't necessarily bad for the big labs. They get productive years from talented people, and the alumni ecosystem creates a network that can be valuable for recruiting, partnerships, and information flow. But it does mean that the frontier of AI research is increasingly distributed rather than concentrated.

For practitioners, this matters because it affects where innovation happens. If you're trying to stay current on what's coming next in AI tooling, you can't just watch Google and OpenAI. You need to track the startups founded by their alumni — because that's where some of the most ambitious bets are being placed.

## What We Don't Know

There's a lot we don't know about these departures, and I want to be careful not to overinterpret sparse information.

We don't know the specific research agenda the new company will pursue. "Discovery loop methodology" is a phrase, not a roadmap.

We don't know how the departures are being received internally at DeepMind. There's a difference between amicable parting and quiet relief.

We don't know whether the researchers' critiques of Google's priorities are accurate or whether they're rationalizing a decision they made for other reasons — compensation, restlessness, the appeal of founding something.

We don't know whether the new company has funding, what its structure looks like, or when it might produce anything usable.

What we do know is that four people with deep experience in cutting-edge AI research looked at their options and decided they could do better outside Google. That's a signal worth paying attention to, even if we're not sure exactly what it means.

## [CHRIS TAKE]

## What to Watch

**Watch for announcements from the new venture.** The discovery loop researchers will presumably need to explain what they're building eventually, and the framing they choose will reveal a lot about their actual agenda.

**Watch for Google's response.** If DeepMind doubles down on long-term research — more publications, more speculative projects, more tolerance for ambiguity — it suggests they see the departures as a problem to address. If nothing changes, it suggests they've accepted this as the cost of their current strategy.

**Watch for similar departures at other labs.** If this is a one-off event, it's just personnel movement. If it's the start of a trend, it signals something deeper about how AI research gets done at scale.

**Watch your own assumptions.** If you've been assuming that Google will remain at the frontier of AI capabilities indefinitely, these departures are a reminder that the people who create those capabilities have their own priorities — and those priorities don't always align with corporate strategy.

## What to Do Next

If you're making decisions about AI tooling for your team, this doesn't change much in the short term. Gemini isn't going anywhere. Google's AI products will continue to improve. The departures of four researchers, however talented, don't invalidate the work of thousands of others.

But if you're thinking about the medium term — where AI capabilities will be in three to five years — it's worth considering that the answer might not be "wherever Google is." The people most committed to pushing boundaries are increasingly distributed across startups, smaller labs, and independent research efforts.

This has implications for how you stay current. Reading Google's blog posts isn't enough. You need to track the broader ecosystem, including the ventures founded by people who left.

It also has implications for how you evaluate vendor claims. When Google or any other large company promises breakthrough capabilities, ask yourself: who's actually doing the research? Are the people responsible for past breakthroughs still there? And if not, where did they go?

---

Here's what I keep coming back to: if four researchers left because they wanted to "build something differently," what exactly do they think is different about how they'll do it? Is this about methodology, or is this about incentives? And if it's about incentives — if the structure of big companies makes certain kinds of research structurally impossible — what does that mean for everyone betting on those companies to deliver the next generation of AI capabilities?
